source_text: Sed cum haec ita sint, quomodo huic opinioni contrarium non sit quod dicit apostolus: omnes enim astabimus ante tribunal Christi, ut ferat unusquisque secundum ea quae per corpus gessit, siue bonum siue malum, non te satis uidere significas. haec quippe apostolica sententia ante mortem admonet fieri quod possit prodesse post mortem. non tunc, quando iam recipiendum est quod quisque gesserit ante mortem. uerum haec ita soluitur quaestio, quoniam quodam uitae genere adquiritur, dum in hoc corpore uiuitur, ut aliquid adiuuent ista defunctos, ac per hoc secundum ea quae per corpus gesserunt eis quae post corpus religiose pro illis facta fuerint adiuuantur. sunt enim, quos nihil omnino adiuuant ista, siue pro eis fiant, quorum tam mala sunt merita, ut nec talibus digni sint adiuuari, siue pro eis, quorum tam bona, ut talibus non indigeant adiumentis. genere igitur uitae, quod gessit quisque per corpus. efficitur, ut prosint uel non prosint, quaecumque pro illo pie fiunt, cum reliquerit corpus. nam meritum per quod ista prosint, si nullum conparatum est in hac uita, frustra post hanc quaeritur uitam. ita fit, ut neque inaniter ecclesia uel suorum cura pro defunctis quod potuerit religionis inpendat et tamen ferat unusquisque secundum ea quae per corpus gessit, siue bonum siue malum reddente domino unicuique secundum opera eius. ut enim hoc, quod inpenditur, possit ei prodesse post corpus, in ea uita est adquisitum, quam gessit in corpore.
thought_title: Life's merit decides whether posthumous rites help
orientation: Augustine is answering Paulinus's worry that his view about burial and prayers for the dead might conflict with Paul's statement that each person will be repaid for what he did in the body.
pass_a_gloss: But since these things are so, how it is not contrary to this opinion what the apostle says: for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive according to the things which he did through the body, whether good or evil, you indicate that you do not sufficiently see. This apostolic sentence indeed admonishes that before death be done what can profit after death. Not then, when already what each one did before death is to be received. But this question is solved in this way, because by a certain kind of life it is acquired, while one lives in this body, that these things help the dead somewhat, and through this according to the things which they did through the body they are helped by the things which after the body are done religiously for them. For there are those whom these things help not at all, whether they are done for those whose merits are so bad that they are not worthy to be helped by such things, or for those whose merits are so good that they do not need such helps. Therefore by the kind of life, which each one led through the body, it is brought about that whatever things are done piously for him profit or do not profit, when he has left the body. For if no merit through which these things profit was acquired in this life, it is sought in vain after this life. So it happens that neither in vain does the church or the care of their own people spend what it can of religious duty for the dead, and yet each one receives according to the things which he did through the body, whether good or evil, the Lord repaying each one according to his works. For in order that this, which is spent, may be able to profit him after the body, it was acquired in that life which he led in the body.

choices.why: Standard English for the Pauline tribunal imagery; keeps the forensic sense of the Latin.
Literal rendering preserves the Pauline phrase's emphasis on bodily life as the sphere of moral action.
Keeps the adverbial force and the sense of acts of religious duty done for the dead.
The verb means to expend or lay out; it fits the idea of the church expending effort and religious care.

choices.term: reddente domino unicuique secundum opera eius
choices.english: the Lord repaying each one according to his works
choices.why: Echoes the biblical language of divine recompense; keeps the ablative absolute as a clause.
rejected: with the Lord giving back to each according to his deeds

bible_refs.note: omnes enim astabimus ante tribunal Christi, ut ferat unusquisque secundum ea quae per corpus gessit, siue bonum siue malum
reddente domino unicuique secundum opera eius

pass_b_english: But since this is so, you indicate that you do not quite see how the apostle's saying is not contrary to this opinion: "For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what he did through the body, whether good or evil" (2 Corinthians 5:10). This apostolic sentence warns that what can help after death should be done before death, not at the time when each person must already receive what he did before death. But the question is solved this way: by a certain kind of life something is acquired while one lives in this body, so that these things may help the dead somewhat. And so, according to what they did through the body, they are helped by the things that are religiously done for them after the body. For there are some whom these things do not help at all—whether they are done for those whose merits are so evil that they are not worthy to be helped by such things, or for those whose merits are so good that they do not need such helps. Therefore, by the kind of life that each one led through the body, it comes about that whatever is piously done for him after he has left the body helps or does not help. For if no merit by which these things help was acquired in this life, it is sought in vain after this life. So it happens that neither the church nor the care of one's own people spends its religious effort for the dead in vain, and yet each one receives according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil, the Lord repaying each one according to his works (Romans 2:6). For in order that what is spent may help him after the body, it was acquired in that life which he led in the body.

problems.quote: not at the time when each person is already about to receive what he did before death
problems.source_quote: non tunc, quando iam recipiendum est quod quisque gesserit ante mortem
problems.why: 'recipiendum est' means 'must be received/repaid,' not 'about to receive'; 'quod quisque gesserit' is the object received, not what he did
problems.fix: not then, when each person must already receive what he did before death
problems.ruling: 'recipiendum est' is passive necessity 'must be received,' not 'about to receive'; 'quod gesserit' is object, not 'what he did'

problems.source_quote: omnes enim astabimus ante tribunal Christi, ut ferat unusquisque secundum ea quae per corpus gessit, siue bonum siue malum
problems.why: The verse quoted is actually Romans 14:10 or 2 Corinthians 5:10, but Augustine's text reads 'astabimus' (we shall stand), which matches Romans 14:10 (Vulgate: 'omnes enim stabimus ante tribunal Christi'), not 2 Cor 5:10 (Vulgate: 'omnes enim nos manifestari oportet ante tribunal Christi'). The citation should be Romans 14:10.
problems.ruling: Source 'astabimus' matches Romans 14:10, not 2 Cor 5:10; wrong scripture reference misleads reader.

edits.old: not at the time when each person is already about to receive what he did before death
edits.new: not at the time when each person must already receive what he did before death

fixed: Changed 'about to receive' to 'must already receive' to match 'recipiendum est' (gerundive of obligation), and 'what he did before death' is the object received.
Changed the citation from 2 Corinthians 5:10 to Romans 14:10, since Augustine's text reads 'astabimus' (we shall stand), which matches Romans 14:10 rather than 2 Corinthians 5:10.

problems.source_quote: omnes enim astabimus ante tribunal Christi, ut ferat unusquisque secundum ea quae per corpus gessit, siue bonum siue malum
problems.why: The verse quoted matches 2 Corinthians 5:10, not Romans 14:10. Romans 14:10 says 'we shall all stand before the judgment seat of God/Christ' but lacks 'receive according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil.'
problems.ruling: Source 'ut ferat unusquisque secundum ea quae per corpus gessit' matches 2 Cor 5:10, not Romans 14:10.

fixed: The verse quoted matches 2 Corinthians 5:10, not Romans 14:10; the citation has been corrected.

problems.quote: so that these things may help the dead
problems.why: Missing 'aliquid' = 'something': the sense is 'so that these things may help the dead in some respect/to some degree', not absolutely 'help the dead'. The 'aliquid' is significant—it means the post-mortem helps are partial, not the main thing.
problems.fix: so that these things may help the dead somewhat

problems.quote: a certain kind of life is acquired
problems.source_quote: quoniam quodam uitae genere adquiritur, dum in hoc corpore uiuitur
problems.why: Subject is wrong: 'adquiritur' is passive but the sense is 'one acquires by a certain kind of life' or 'a certain kind of life is acquired [by one]'. The English makes it sound like life itself is acquired, but 'genere uitae' is instrumental/ablative of manner: 'by a certain kind of life'. The meaning is 'because by a certain kind of life it is acquired, while one lives in this body'—i.e., merit is acquired by living a certain kind of life.
problems.fix: because by a certain kind of life something is acquired while one lives in this body
problems.ruling: 'quodam uitae genere' is ablative of means; 'adquiritur' passive. Meaning is 'by a kind of life it is acquired,' not 'a kind of life is acquired.'

edits.old: so that these things may help the dead.
edits.new: so that these things may help the dead somewhat.

edits.old: a certain kind of life is acquired while one lives in this body
edits.new: by a certain kind of life something is acquired while one lives in this body

fixed: Added 'somewhat' to render 'aliquid' (source: 'ut aliquid adiuuent ista defunctos').

Changed 'a certain kind of life is acquired' to 'by a certain kind of life something is acquired' to render the instrumental ablative 'quodam uitae genere' (source: 'quoniam quodam uitae genere adquiritur, dum in hoc corpore uiuitur').

dismissed.why: The verse quoted is Romans 14:10/2 Corinthians 5:10, but Augustine's citation matches Romans 14:10 more closely ('astabimus' = 'we shall stand,' found in Romans 14:10 OL; 2 Cor 5:10 has 'manifestari' in Vulgate). The parenthetical should be Romans 14:10.
dismissed.note: 'ut ferat unusquisque… per corpus… siue bonum siue malum' is 2 Corinthians 5:10; the Old Latin wording of the opening does not make it Romans 14:10.
